summaries.example: Imagine looking at a red apple. It may seem round, shiny, and close to you. Your experience gives you information about the apple. But if the apple is actually green, or if you are seeing it in a mirror, your experience may be misleading. Philosophers ask whether the experience itself is inaccurate, or whether only the belief you form from it is inaccurate.
summaries.summary: The contents of perception are what our sensory experiences seem to tell us. When you look at something, it may appear to have a shape, color, size, location, or texture. The experience can give you this information even when the information is mistaken. For example, a reflection can make a fish seem to be in front of you when it is actually behind you. Philosophers call the ways an experience can get things right its accuracy conditions. They disagree about whether experiences really have such conditions. Some say experiences represent the world and can be accurate or inaccurate. Others say experiences are feelings, ways of being affected, or relations to things, and that only later beliefs can be true or false. The entry also examines how experiences relate to beliefs, how different senses present space and objects, and whether experiences need concepts. It asks how the felt character of experience connects with what the experience represents.
key_ideas: Seeing, hearing, touching, tasting, smelling, and sensing body movement all involve experiences with a particular felt character.
Many philosophers think an experience has content when it presents the world as being a certain way.
An experience may seem to show something that is not really there or not really the way it appears.
Some philosophers deny that experiences themselves can be true or false. They say that only the beliefs formed from experiences can be accurate or inaccurate.
Philosophers also ask whether experiences are connected to beliefs, whether they use concepts, and whether their content comes partly from the surrounding world.
summaries.why_it_matters: Our senses help us learn about the world, but they can also mislead us. Understanding perceptual content helps explain why a reflection, strange sound, or body sensation can seem convincing even when it is mistaken. It also helps us think carefully about the difference between what we experience, what we believe, and what is actually true.

important_terms.definition: What a perceptual experience tells or seems to tell you about the world.
What it is like to have an experience, such as seeing red or feeling pressure.
A condition that must be true for an experience to get things right.
An experience that does not match how things really are.

questions_to_think_about: If a stick looks bent in water, is the seeing itself wrong, or only your judgment about the stick?
Can a baby or animal have a rich experience without having words for what it senses?
Does seeing a red apple include seeing an apple, or only seeing red and round shapes in a place?
Can two people have the same kind of experience even when they are looking at different objects?

summaries.example: Suppose you see a red cube through a mirror. The cube you are seeing is orange and behind you, but a different red cube happens to be located where the reflected cube appears to be. Several theories give different verdicts. An object-involving theory says the experience is inaccurate because the cube you see is not red and is not in front of you. A simpler existential theory says the experience may be accurate because there is a red cube at the apparent location. A theory using a gap in its content can preserve the idea that the particular cube you see matters without treating the content as a direct relation to that cube.
summaries.summary: Perceptual experience has a distinctive phenomenal character: there is something it is like to see, hear, touch, taste, smell, or sense bodily movement. The philosophical question is what, if anything, these experiences represent. On the dominant contemporary approach, perceptual content is tied to accuracy conditions. An experience of a red cube, for example, is accurate under circumstances in which relevant objects and properties are arranged as the experience presents them. Yet this approach is controversial. Some philosophers hold that experience is a raw sensory condition, a modification of the subject, or a relation to a particular environmental object, and therefore is not itself assessable as true or false. Others connect experience to belief by identifying it with belief acquisition, a disposition to form a belief, or a perceptual ground for such a disposition. A separate approach treats experience as an attitude toward content, while leaving open what an experiential attitude consists in. Theories of content then face several constraints. They must explain intuitions about illusion and hallucination, preserve relevant differences in phenomenology, and handle perspective-sensitive features such as left, right, here, and now. Russellian contents use objects and properties; Fregean contents use modes of presentation; possible-worlds theories use sets of ways the world could be; and indexical theories introduce centered or gappy structures. Some theories assign multiple contents because no single kind seems able to explain all the relevant phenomena. Further disputes concern whether high-level properties, ordinary objects, causal relations, absences, affordances, or mind-independence are represented in experience. key_ideas: The entry uses content mainly in an informational sense: the content of an experience is connected with the conditions under which it is accurate, not with items literally located inside the mind.

Whether experiences have accuracy conditions is a substantive dispute. Views that reject them include raw-feel theories, forms of adverbialism, some versions of naïve realism, and some sense-datum theories.
A theory of perceptual content must account both for veridicality and for phenomenology: it should explain when experiences are correct and why different experiences feel different.
Proposed contents include object-involving, existential, gappy, Russellian, Fregean, possible-worlds, centered-world, and multiple-content theories.

A major debate concerns whether experiences require concepts. Conceptualists connect experience content with concepts, while non-conceptualist views emphasize the richness or fine-grained detail of perception.
Philosophers also disagree about whether content determines phenomenology, whether phenomenology determines content, and whether content depends on internal properties, external relations, or both.
summaries.why_it_matters: The theory of perceptual content connects basic sensory life with knowledge, belief, action, and consciousness. It helps explain how perception can guide behavior while still being fallible, why different sensory modalities may have different kinds of content, and why the same apparent scene can be interpreted differently. The debate also tests broader theories of the mind: whether mental representation is fundamentally internal, environmentally grounded, concept-dependent, or rooted in phenomenal character.

important_terms.definition: A way of having a mental state, such as believing, hoping, desiring, or experiencing something perceptually.
A structured content containing an object and a property, such as a particular cube being red.
A content made from ways an object or property is presented, allowing one thing to be presented in different ways.
Content that represents something relative to the perceiver, such as “to my left,” “here,” or “now.”
The view that experiences can represent without requiring the subject to possess all the relevant concepts.
The thesis that phenomenal character is determined by representational properties.
The view that experience content can depend partly on relations to the environment outside the subject.
The idea that some experiential content is fixed by phenomenology itself.

questions_to_think_about: Should an experience itself be called inaccurate, or should inaccuracy belong only to the belief formed from it?
If two people have phenomenally similar experiences of different objects, must their contents be the same?
Can a subject represent a precise shade or spatial relation without possessing a matching concept?
Does visual experience represent ordinary objects, or only colors, shapes, depths, and other lower-level features?
Could the same content feel different when presented visually, tactually, or through another modality?

summaries.example: You and a friend stand on opposite sides of a room while a bell rings. You hear the sound as coming from your left; your friend hears it as coming from their right. The sound and the place may be the same, but the experiences differ because each one presents the sound from a different point of view. Philosophers call this kind of perspective-sensitive information indexical content. They also ask whether the experience represents the sound’s direction itself, a location relative to your body, or a possible way of moving toward the sound.
summaries.summary: The contents of perception are the ways perceptual experiences present things as being. A visual experience may present a surface as colored, an object as shaped, or something as located in front of the perceiver. Auditory, tactile, gustatory, olfactory, and bodily experiences raise similar questions, although their boundaries and contents may differ. One influential proposal identifies perceptual content with accuracy conditions: an experience is accurate when the world satisfies what it presents. Illusions and hallucinations make this proposal attractive, since they seem to involve appearances that do not match reality. However, the source also describes views that reject accuracy conditions for experience. On these views, experiences may be raw sensations, changes in how a subject is affected, or relations to objects; a false belief caused by an experience, rather than the experience itself, is what is inaccurate. Other theories link experience to belief through belief acquisition, dispositions to believe, or perceptual grounds for belief. A further framework separates content from attitude: the content concerns what is represented, while the attitude concerns how it is entertained. The entry then examines competing accounts of the form of content. Some include objects and properties directly, some use possible situations, and some use modes of presentation. Perspective introduces another challenge. Experiences often represent locations relative to the perceiver, so contents may need indexicals or centered structures. Philosophers also ask whether perception represents ordinary objects, high-level properties, mind-independent things, or only lower-level sensory features. The conceptualism debate asks whether a person must possess concepts in order to have the content
key_ideas: Perceptual experiences have a felt side and may also have an informational or representational side.
The idea that experiences have accuracy conditions is supported by illusions and hallucinations, but it is not accepted by every philosopher.
Beliefs and experiences may be related, but an experience is not obviously the same as a belief: someone can know that an appearance is misleading while still having that appearance.
Perceptual content may represent properties such as color, shape, depth, location, and perhaps higher-level features such as emotion or what someone is doing.
A single theory may not explain every feature of perception, so some philosophers propose that experiences have more than one kind of content.
Philosophers debate whether concepts are necessary for perception and whether perception can contain more detail than a person can think or remember.
summaries.why_it_matters: Perception seems to give us immediate contact with the world, yet it can be mistaken and is shaped by viewpoint, attention, background knowledge, and the sensory system. Studying perceptual content clarifies how sensory experience can support beliefs without simply being identical to belief. It also shows why questions about consciousness, knowledge, action, concepts, and the external world are closely connected.

important_terms.definition: The information or situation that a perception presents, such as an object being red or a sound coming from the left.
The felt quality of an experience—what seeing, hearing, touching, or hurting is like.
The circumstances in which an experience would correctly present the world.
A mental state such as believing, hoping, wanting, or perceiving, considered as a way of relating to content.
Content that depends on a viewpoint, using ideas such as “here,” “now,” “in front of me,” or “to my left.”
Content that can be present in experience even when the person does not possess concepts for every detail represented.
A position claiming that experiences do not represent the world and therefore are not themselves accurate or inaccurate.

questions_to_think_about: When you see a familiar place differently after learning more about it, has the content of your experience changed, its phenomenology changed, or both?
Does a hallucination have the same content as a matching ordinary perception?
If an experience leads you toward a belief, must the experience itself have a truth-like accuracy status?
Can an experience represent a particular object, or does it represent only that some object with certain properties is present?
What should a theory of perception explain first: what an experience feels like, what it represents, or how it causes beliefs and actions?
